In agency work with local businesses, the problem often does not begin with design or with the choice of CMS. The problem is that the agency sells a “website” and then manually maintains the chaos it has created itself.

- If the website is built as a reproducible artifact, the agency’s operating model changes. Content lives in structured files, business data is moved into canonical locations, the build validates changes, and the release follows a clear cycle. This is not about adding complexity for the sake of engineering aesthetics. It is about reducing dependence on the memory of a specific developer and on manual checks after every small edit.

- For a productized web service, constraints matter. A design system with tokens, a ban on hard-coded colors, and safeguards against weak visual clichés sounds less appealing than full editorial freedom. But freedom often turns into technical debt and communication noise. In a service model for small businesses, constraints can be part of the value because they protect the system from accidental degradation.

- The most mature element here is honest economics. Not claiming that this model is cheaper than any CMS. Not selling search visibility as a promise. Not presenting architectural discipline as legal compliance. It is useful for an agency to separate what the system actually controls from what requires an audit, manual review, or separate expertise.

How would you package such a model: as website development, as an infrastructure subscription, or as an operational service for local businesses?
